issues.legal_issue: Interpreting documents relied on to establish ownership may raise a substantial question of law in a second appeal, and the appeal cannot be dismissed as involving only factual questions without considering and framing the relevant substantial questions of law.
material_facts: A public body and the government each claimed ownership of the same land.
The parties relied on documentary evidence to establish their respective titles, and the courts below made findings on ownership.
The High Court dismissed the second appeal in limine, treating the findings as pure findings of fact, without framing substantial questions of law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court committed a jurisdictional error by dismissing the second appeal as involving only questions of fact. It was required to admit the appeal, frame appropriate substantial questions of law concerning the interpretation of the ownership documents, and decide the appeal on its merits after hearing the parties.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal must be admitted and decided on substantial questions of law. Where deciding ownership requires proper interpretation of documents, particularly admitted documents, the issue involves a legal question rather than merely a question of fact. The High Court must frame specific substantial questions of law relevant to the documents and the alleged errors in the findings below. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: second_appeal and ownership_disputed and document_interpretation_required and high_court_dismissed_as_pure_fact

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from decisions of the courts below.
predicates.ownership_disputed: The parties claim competing ownership rights over the same property.
predicates.document_interpretation_required: Determining ownership requires interpreting documents relied on by the parties.
predicates.high_court_dismissed_as_pure_fact: The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the findings were factual, without framing substantial questions of law.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns disputed ownership that requires interpretation of the parties’ documents, a dismissal as purely factual without framing substantial questions of law requires the High Court to admit the appeal, frame those questions, and decide it on the merits.

issues.legal_issue: In a civil suit or proceeding to which the government is a party, the court must first endeavor to assist the parties in reaching a settlement where that is possible consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case, before finally deciding the merits.
material_facts: The case concerned a civil suit between the government and a statutory public body asserting competing ownership rights over land.
No endeavor by the court or the parties to reach a settlement was made.
The courts decided the dispute on its merits without a reported failure of settlement efforts.
issues.conclusion: The court should have endeavored to assist the parties in reaching a settlement and should have finally decided the case on its merits only after failure of those efforts was reported.
issues.legal_principle: Order 27 Rule 5B of the Code of Civil Procedure places a duty on the court, in a suit or proceeding involving the government or a public officer acting officially, to make every endeavor in the first instance to assist settlement where possible consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case. If a reasonable possibility of settlement appears at any stage, the court may adjourn the proceeding to enable settlement efforts.

predicates.government_party_civil_proceeding: The proceeding is a civil suit or proceeding to which the government or a public officer acting officially is a party.
predicates.settlement_possible_consistently_with_ca: Settlement efforts are possible consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case.
predicates.merits_decided_without_settlement_effort: The court decides the merits without first endeavoring to assist settlement.

issues.definition: When the government is a party to a civil proceeding and settlement efforts are possible in light of the case, deciding the merits without those efforts means the court must first assist settlement and proceed to a merits decision only after the efforts fail.
